title: Chantilly Arts & Élégance 2026
excerpt: Where the setting becomes part of the spectacle, without ever taking the spotlight away from the cars.

sections.heading: A Different Scale
sections.text:
Even before reaching the heart of the Domaine de Chantilly, it was clear that this would be a very different kind of automotive event.

Cars were already appearing around the entrance to the château, with remarkable machinery parked across a venue that seemed to keep unfolding as we walked further into it. A Lamborghini Gallardo LP 570-4 was among the first cars to catch our attention, but it was only a small indication of what waited beyond.

The scale of Chantilly is difficult to understand until you experience it. The château, gardens and vast lawns provide enough room for hundreds of cars without reducing the event to rows of metal arranged on an exhibition floor. Instead, every part of the Domaine seemed to reveal something different.

And the cars were only one layer of it.

Horse-drawn carriages moved through the grounds. Jugglers, musicians and performers appeared between the crowds. Food stands and activities filled the spaces between the displays, while the official Sunday programme ranged from the Garden Party and concours parades to carriage rides, boating and equestrian entertainment.

The crowd itself became part of that spectacle. Suits, dresses, hats and carefully considered outfits were everywhere, some visitors appearing almost as meticulously presented as the cars standing beside them.

Yet remarkably, none of it felt forced.

There was an unmistakably aristocratic atmosphere to Chantilly, but without the sense that luxury was being performed simply for its own sake. The clothes, the people, the château and the cars all seemed to belong in the same picture.

English, French and Spanish conversations mixed together as we moved through a crowd that felt noticeably international.

For a day, the entire Domaine had become the event.

sections.heading: Where Elegance Meets the Automobile
sections.text:
What makes Chantilly particularly impressive is how naturally the automotive world fits into its surroundings.

Ferrari, Porsche, Alpine, Bugatti and countless historic machines were spread across the estate, while clubs and collectors transformed the lawns into something closer to a temporary open-air automotive museum. The 2026 field ranged from pre-war machinery to GT1 racers and modern one-offs, but the diversity never made the event feel incoherent.

At another event, an exceptional car can sometimes feel like an object simply placed on a stand.

At Chantilly, the environment becomes part of its presentation.

The château rises behind the cars. The gardens extend beyond them. Historic architecture, water, trees and carefully arranged lawns provide a backdrop that would be almost impossible to reproduce elsewhere.

Yet the setting never overwhelms what has come to occupy it.

That balance is perhaps the most remarkable part of Chantilly. There is an enormous amount competing for your attention, the people, the architecture, the fashion, the scale of the Domaine itself, but the cars somehow remain at the centre of everything.

And that becomes even more apparent when you start recognising exactly what is in front of you.

A Ferrari may be one of several dozen on the grounds until you realise the next lawn holds a competition car with its own racing history. A Porsche may initially disappear among the crowds until another angle reveals something much rarer. At Chantilly, curiosity is rewarded constantly.

Nothing feels excessive simply for the sake of being excessive.

Nothing feels fake.

Instead, prestige, automotive history and contemporary performance seem to coexist naturally.

You feel absorbed into the event simply by walking through it, but never get the impression that the visitors themselves are supposed to be the main attraction.

We are part of the scene.

The cars are the reason it exists.

sections.heading: Bugatti, in Formation
sections.text:
Among everything we encountered that Sunday, one display stood above almost everything else.

Bugatti.

At its centre was the Brouillard, the first one-of-one creation of Bugatti's Programme Solitaire and one of the most anticipated cars of the weekend. More than another heavily personalised Bugatti, Solitaire represents the marque’s return to creating individual coachbuilt interpretations around its existing engineering. Commissioned for the Perridon Collection, its presence alone would have been enough to make the Bugatti area memorable. And actually, Chantilly was where Brouillard was formally handed over to its owner before later taking the Best of Show award for Concept Cars, Restomods & One-Offs.

But it was surrounded by a line-up that could have formed an event of its own.

Two W16 Mistrals.

One of the two W16 Mistrals was Le Retour du Jeune Prince, a one-off Sur Mesure commission built around the owner’s own literary continuation of The Little Prince, with its copper-and-bronze finish and constellation-inspired detailing turning the car into something far more personal than a conventional specification.

Beside it sat the W16 Mistral World Record Car, representing a completely different side of the same model, while Bugatti also brought the Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse World Record Car and the specially restored Veyron La Maison Pur Sang 20 Years. The weekend also saw three Veyrons and the one-off Chiron Profilée take part in a rally around Chantilly

A Chiron.

Five Veyrons.

Different chapters of modern Bugatti history sitting only metres apart, with the Brouillard representing the marque's latest exploration of bespoke coachbuilding.

Seeing them together gave the display a significance that went beyond individual specifications.

The Veyron changed the limits of the modern production car. The Chiron pushed that philosophy further. The Mistral became the final expression of Bugatti's W16 era, while the Brouillard represented something considerably more individual and bespoke.

And against the Domaine de Chantilly, they somehow looked entirely at home.

The display was one of those rare occasions where it was almost difficult to decide what to photograph first. Wide enough to capture the entire line-up, close enough to study the details, then back again as another angle revealed itself.

Ferrari, Porsche and countless other remarkable cars surrounded them throughout the day, but whenever we returned to the Bugatti display, it still felt special.

And impressive as they were standing still, the moment that ultimately defined our experience of Chantilly was still to come.

sections.heading: When the Engines Took Over
sections.text:
Eventually, the Bugattis began to leave their display.

One by one, engines fired into life.

The crowd shifted towards the route. Cameras came up. Cars that had spent much of the afternoon being examined almost like pieces of sculpture suddenly reminded everyone that they were machines designed to move.

Hearing them start was already enough to change the atmosphere.

Watching them appear together was something else entirely.

The Brouillard moved towards the parade alongside the rest of the Bugatti line-up, including pre-war cars from the marque's history, and for a few minutes everything that made Chantilly distinctive seemed to exist within the same scene.

Bugattis moving together.

The gardens behind them.

The water stretching alongside the route.

Sails and flags visible in the distance.

People lining the edge of the parade.

It became one of those rare automotive moments where the location matters almost as much as the cars themselves.

Shortly afterwards came another spectacle: a parade of Ferrari F40s, their familiar silhouettes moving through the same environment and replacing the polished stillness of the concours with sound, movement and theatre.

That contrast ultimately defined Chantilly for us.

For most of the day, the cars could be studied in extraordinary surroundings, surrounded by elegant crowds, architecture, gardens and a carefully curated atmosphere.

Then the engines started.

And everything else briefly became background.

Despite its scale, its prestige and the thousands of people moving through the Domaine, Chantilly never seemed to forget what should occupy the centre of the experience.

The château is spectacular.

The setting is extraordinary.

The atmosphere is unique.

But the cars are what bring it to life.
